title: How do you do a back-of-envelope capacity estimate in a system-design interview (QPS, storage/day→/year, bandwidth, cache size, and the latency numbers every engineer should know)?
shortTitle: How do you do a back-of-envelope capacity estimate in a system-design interview?
keyPoints: QPS: daily active users x actions/day / 86400 seconds, then multiply by peak factor (2-5x).
Storage: per-record size x daily writes x 365 x retention years, plus index and replication overhead.
Bandwidth: peak QPS x response size; reveals whether a CDN is needed.
Cache size: hot fraction (Pareto 20%) x item size x distinct items.
Latency numbers: memory ~100 ns, SSD ~100 us, same-DC round trip ~500 us, cross-continent ~150 ms.
Split read/write QPS by the read-to-write ratio to place caches and replicas.
The estimate drives architecture: QPS sizes the fleet, storage decides sharding, bandwidth decides CDN.

s1_definition.oneliner: Back-of-envelope estimation turns daily active users into QPS, bytes per day into bytes per year, rate times payload into bandwidth, and the hot fraction into cache size, all anchored by the latency numbers every engineer should know.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **QPS** -- daily active users x actions/day / ~100K seconds/day, then multiply by peak factor.
- **Storage** -- per-record bytes x daily writes x 365 x retention, plus indexes (~2x) and replication.
- **Bandwidth** -- peak QPS x response size (bytes to bits to Mbps/Gbps).
- **Cache** -- hot 20% of items x item size; check it fits a Redis node.
- **Latency numbers** -- memory ~100 ns, SSD ~100 us, same-DC ~500 us, cross-continent ~150 ms.
- **Read/write split** -- reads go to caches/replicas; writes hit the primary.
s1_definition.analogy: Before opening a new branch, the National Bank of India manager scribbles on an envelope: 10,000 customers, 2 visits per month, 700 visits per day, peak triple that at lunch, so size for 2,000 visits per hour. Estimate paper storage per year, and check if the vault is big enough. Same math, scaled to servers, storage, and cache.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Back-of-Envelope Flow

  Input: 10M DAU, 5 actions/day
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ QPS: 10M x 5 / 100K = 500 avg         │
  │      x 4 peak factor = 2000 peak      │
  ├────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Storage: 1KB x 50M/day = 50 GB/day    │
  │          x 365 = 18 TB/year           │
  │          x 5 years x 2 (indexes)      │
  │          = 180 TB --> NEEDS SHARDING   │
  ├────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Bandwidth: 2000 x 2KB = 4 MB/s (32Mb) │
  │            --> single NIC OK           │
  ├────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Cache: 20% of 10M x 1KB = 2 GB        │
  │        --> one Redis node              │
  └────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Estimate --> Architecture
  QPS        --> fleet size
  Storage    --> sharding
  Bandwidth  --> CDN?
  Cache      --> Redis topology
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A back-of-envelope capacity estimate grounds an architecture in physical reality. You derive QPS from daily active users and actions, scale daily storage to yearly, compute bandwidth from rate times payload, and size the cache from the hot fraction. The latency numbers anchor everything: memory is roughly 1,000 times faster than SSD, SSD is 1,000 times faster than HDD seek, and a cross-continent round trip is 150 ms no matter how fast the server.

The estimate drives architecture decisions: QPS sizes the fleet, storage per year decides sharding, the read/write split places caches and replicas, bandwidth decides whether a CDN is mandatory, and the latency numbers keep slow cross-region calls off the critical path.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj estimated a transaction-history service: 10M DAU at 5 actions gave 500 average and 2,000 peak QPS, the write volume projected to over 160 TB with indexes so it needed sharding, and the hot 20% of accounts fit in about 2 GB of Redis on one node.

Remember one sentence: turn users and actions into QPS, bytes per day into bytes per year, rate times payload into bandwidth, and the hot fraction into cache size, all anchored by the latency numbers, because the right power of ten tells you whether you need one server or a thousand.
